questions.problem: Find $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ for $f(x,y)=\operatorname{tan}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{tan}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))) \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)) \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))\cdot \frac{1}{x+y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{sec}^{2}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))\cdot \frac{1}{x+y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y) & =\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))}{x+y}\cdot (x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(1)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)) \\  & =\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))}{x+y}\cdot (x\cdot 0+1) \\  & =\frac{{sec}^{2}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))}{x+y}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{3}y).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+{x}^{3}y)) \\  & =\frac{1}{x+{x}^{3}y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+{x}^{3}y)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the sum and constant multiple rules for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x+{x}^{3}y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+{x}^{3}y) & =\frac{1}{x+{x}^{3}y}\cdot (\frac{∂}{∂x}(x)+y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3})) \\  & =\frac{1}{x+{x}^{3}y}\cdot (1+y\cdot 3{x}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1+3{x}^{2}y}{x+{x}^{3}y}\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x+1)^{{y}^{2}}) \\  & ={y}^{2}(x+1)^{{y}^{2}-1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the sum rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}(x+1)^{{y}^{2}-1}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+1) & ={y}^{2}(x+1)^{{y}^{2}-1}\cdot (\frac{∂}{∂x}(x)+\frac{∂}{∂x}(1)) \\  & ={y}^{2}(x+1)^{{y}^{2}-1}\cdot (1+0) \\  & ={y}^{2}(x+1)^{{y}^{2}-1}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ for $f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1}).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{2xy-1}) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2xy-1}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the sum and the constant multiple rules for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2xy-1}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy-1) & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})}{2\sqrt{2xy-1}}(2x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y)-\frac{∂}{∂y}(1)) \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})}{2\sqrt{2xy-1}}\cdot (2x\cdot 1-0) \\  & =-\frac{x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2xy-1})}{\sqrt{2xy-1}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y)={x}^{3}{y}^{2}+{e}^{xy},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(-1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}+{e}^{xy}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{xy})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the chain rule and constant multiple rules for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2})+{e}^{xy}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(xy) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3})+{e}^{xy}\cdot y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot 3{x}^{2}+{e}^{xy}\cdot y\cdot 1 \\  & =3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+y{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(-1,1)} & =3(-1)^{2}(1)^{2}+(1){e}^{(-1)(1)} \\  & =3+{e}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y)=y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},$ evaluate ${f}_{y}(2,\sqrt{5}).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)\cdot \sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the chain, the sum, and the constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)\cdot \sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}) & =1\cdot \sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+y\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) \\  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\frac{y}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot ({x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(1)+\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2})) \\  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\frac{y}{2\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\cdot ({x}^{2}\cdot 0+2y) \\  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(2,\sqrt{5}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(2,\sqrt{5})} & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{(\sqrt{5})}^{2}}+\frac{{(\sqrt{5})}^{2}}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{(\sqrt{5})}^{2}}} \\  & =\sqrt{4+5}+\frac{5}{\sqrt{4+5}} \\  & =3+\frac{5}{3} \\  & =\frac{14}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ for $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{y}^{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+{y}^{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+{y}^{5}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+{y}^{5}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) & =(\frac{∂}{∂x}(x)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x+x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x))+{y}^{5}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =((1)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x+x\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x))+{y}^{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x-x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+{y}^{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\  & =(1+{y}^{5})\operatorname{cos}⁡x-x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡(x{y}^{2}),$ evaluate ${f}_{x}(\frac{\pi }{4},1)$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡(x{y}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡(x{y}^{2})+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡(x{y}^{2}))\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the chain and the constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡(x{y}^{2})+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{tan}⁡(x{y}^{2})) & =(2x)\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡(x{y}^{2})+{x}^{2}\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡(x{y}^{2})\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}) \\  & =2x\operatorname{tan}⁡(x{y}^{2})+{x}^{2}{sec}^{2}⁡(x{y}^{2})\cdot {y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & =2x\operatorname{tan}⁡(x{y}^{2})+{x}^{2}{sec}^{2}⁡(x{y}^{2})\cdot {y}^{2}\cdot (1) \\  & =2x\operatorname{tan}⁡(x{y}^{2})+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{sec}^{2}⁡(x{y}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(\frac{\pi }{4},1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(\pi /4,1)} & =2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}\cdot \operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot {1}^{2})+{(\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}\cdot {1}^{2}\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot {1}^{2}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}\cdot 1+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{16}\cdot (\sqrt{2})^{2} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{8} \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}+4\pi }{8}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y)={y}^{2}{e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x,$ evaluate ${f}_{y}(0,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the constant multiple rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}{e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}{e}^{y})\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}{e}^{y}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x(\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2})\cdot {e}^{y}+{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{y})) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x((2y)\cdot {e}^{y}+{y}^{2}\cdot {e}^{y}) \\  & =(2y+{y}^{2}){e}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(0,2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y}{|}_{(0,2)} & =(2\cdot 2+{2}^{2}){e}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =8{e}^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =8{e}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+x\sqrt{y},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(\frac{1}{4},4).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+x\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))+\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\sqrt{y}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))+\sqrt{y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the product, the chain, and the constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))+\sqrt{y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) & =(\frac{∂}{∂x}(x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)))+\sqrt{y}\cdot (1) \\  & =(1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+x\cdot \frac{1}{xy}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(xy))+\sqrt{y} \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+\frac{1}{y}\cdot y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x))+\sqrt{y} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)+1+\sqrt{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(\frac{1}{4},4):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(1/4,4)} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{4}\cdot 4)+1+\sqrt{4} \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+1+2 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y}.$ The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is given by

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{h(x,y)}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y)^{2}}.
$$

Find the function $h(x,y).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the quotient rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y}) \\  & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y)-(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y)}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡y\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y)-(\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y-\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡y}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
h(x,y)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{{e}^{y-x}},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(1,-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the quotient and chain rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{{e}^{y-x}}) & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\cdot {e}^{y-x}-({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{y-x})}{{({e}^{y-x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2x\cdot {e}^{y-x}-({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\cdot {e}^{y-x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(y-x)}{{({e}^{y-x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2x{e}^{y-x}-({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\cdot {e}^{y-x}\cdot (-1)}{{({e}^{y-x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(2x+{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}){e}^{y-x}}{{({e}^{y-x})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2x+{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{{e}^{y-x}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,-1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(1,-1)} & =\frac{2(1)+{1}^{2}-(-1)^{2}}{{e}^{-1-1}} \\  & =\frac{2+1-1}{{e}^{-2}} \\  & =2{e}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the function $f(x,y)=\frac{3x+y}{\sqrt{x+y}}.$ The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ is given by

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{h(x,y)}{2(x+y)\sqrt{x+y}}.
$$

Find the function $h(x,y).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the quotient and chain rules, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{3x+y}{\sqrt{x+y}}) \\  & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂x}(3x+y)\cdot \sqrt{x+y}-(3x+y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{x+y})}{{(\sqrt{x+y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(3\cdot \sqrt{x+y}-(3x+y)\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y))}{{(\sqrt{x+y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(3\cdot \sqrt{x+y}-(3x+y)\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y}}\cdot 1)}{{(\sqrt{x+y})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{6(x+y)-(3x+y)}{2\sqrt{x+y}})}{x+y} \\  & =\frac{3x+5y}{2(x+y)\sqrt{x+y}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
h(x,y)=3x+5y.
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡y}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ at the point $(\pi ,-\pi ).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡y}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y}) & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)-(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡y\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)-(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡y)}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡y+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y+\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(\pi ,-\pi ):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(\pi ,-\pi )} & =\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(-\pi )}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi ))^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2(-1)(-1)}{(-1-0)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{1} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y)=\frac{x+y}{\operatorname{sin}⁡y},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂y}$ at the point $(\pi ,\frac{\pi }{2}).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x+y}{\operatorname{sin}⁡y}) & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡y-(x+y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y)}{{sin}^{2}⁡y} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡y-(x+y)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡y}{{sin}^{2}⁡y} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡y-(x+y)\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{{sin}^{2}⁡y}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(\pi ,\frac{\pi }{2}):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(\pi ,\pi /2)} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-(\pi +\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})} \\  & =\frac{1-0}{{1}^{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=x{z}^{3}-{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y),$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(1,1,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{z}^{3}-{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{z}^{3})-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)) \\  & ={z}^{3}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}) \\  & ={z}^{3}\cdot 1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\cdot 2x \\  & ={z}^{3}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(1,1,2)} & ={2}^{3}-2(1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi (1)) \\  & =8-2(1)(-1) \\  & =8+2 \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $g(x,y,z)=\sqrt{x}\operatorname{arccos}⁡(y{z}^{2}),$ evaluate $\frac{∂g}{∂z}$ at the point $(3,\frac{1}{2},1).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $z,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the constant multiple and chain rules, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{x}\operatorname{arccos}⁡(y{z}^{2})) \\  & =\sqrt{x}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{arccos}⁡(y{z}^{2})) \\  & =\sqrt{x}\cdot (-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{(y{z}^{2})}^{2}}})\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(y{z}^{2}) \\  & =\sqrt{x}\cdot (-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}{z}^{4}}})\cdot y\cdot 2z \\  & =-\frac{2yz\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}{z}^{4}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(3,\frac{1}{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂z}{|}_{(3,\,1/2,\,1)} & =-\frac{2(\frac{1}{2})(1)\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{1-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}(1)^{4}}} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{4}}} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})} \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={z}^{2}{e}^{xy}-{y}^{2}{e}^{yz},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂z}$ at the point $(0,-1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $z,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2}{e}^{xy}-{y}^{2}{e}^{yz}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2}{e}^{xy})-\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}{e}^{yz}) \\  & ={e}^{xy}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2})-{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{yz})\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{xy}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2})-{y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{yz}) & ={e}^{xy}\cdot 2z-{y}^{2}\cdot {e}^{yz}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂z}(yz) \\  & ={e}^{xy}\cdot 2z-{y}^{2}\cdot {e}^{yz}\cdot y \\  & =2z{e}^{xy}-{y}^{3}{e}^{yz}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(0,-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂z}{|}_{(0,-1,1)} & =2(1){e}^{(0)(-1)}-(-1)^{3}{e}^{(-1)(1)} \\  & =2+{e}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find ${g}_{y}(x,y,z)$ given that $g(x,y,z)=z\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(xy).$
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

Using the constant multiple and chain rules, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(z\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(xy)) \\  & =z\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(xy)) \\  & =z\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(xy)^{2}}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(xy) \\  & =z\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(xy)^{2}}}\cdot (x) \\  & =\frac{xz}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Partial Derivatives of Three-Variable Functions
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $y,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{3}{y}^{2}-{e}^{2y}{z}^{4}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4{x}^{3}{y}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2y}{z}^{4}) \\  & =4{x}^{3}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2})-{z}^{4}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2y})\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{3}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2})-{z}^{4}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2y}) & =4{x}^{3}\cdot 2y-{z}^{4}\cdot {e}^{2y}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(2y) \\  & =4{x}^{3}\cdot 2y-{z}^{4}\cdot {e}^{2y}\cdot 2 \\  & =8{x}^{3}y-2{z}^{4}{e}^{2y}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{f}_{y}(x,y,z)=8{x}^{3}y-2{z}^{4}{e}^{2y}.
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(y-{x}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{y-{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(y-{x}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{y-{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(y-{x}^{2}) & =\frac{1}{y-{x}^{2}}\cdot (y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(1)-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{y-{x}^{2}}\cdot (y\cdot 0-2x) \\  & =-\frac{2x}{y-{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,9)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,9) & =-\frac{2\cdot 1}{9-{1}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{8} \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the constant multiple rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & =y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x) & =y\cdot (\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\  & =y\cdot ((2x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{x})) \\  & =y(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x) \\  & =xy(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: For the function $f(x,y) = \dfrac{4x-y}{x+y^2},$ evaluate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ at the point $(2,-1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{4x-y}{x+{y}^{2}}) & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x-y)\cdot (x+{y}^{2})-(4x-y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+{y}^{2})}{{(x+{y}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot (x+{y}^{2})-(4x-y)\cdot 1}{{(x+{y}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4x+4{y}^{2}-4x+y}{{(x+{y}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4{y}^{2}+y}{{(x+{y}^{2})}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Then, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(2,-1)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(2,-1)} & =\frac{4(-1)^{2}+(-1)}{{(2+{(-1)}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4-1}{{3}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: For the function  $g(x,y,z) = 2 (x + 1)e^z+ yz,$  evaluate  $\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial z}$ at $(1,1,1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $z,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(2(x+1){e}^{z}+yz) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(2(x+1){e}^{z})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(yz) \\  & =2(x+1)\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{z})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(yz) \\  & =2(x+1){e}^{z}+y\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂z}{|}_{(1,1,1)} & =2(1+1){e}^{1}+1 \\  & =4e+1\end{aligned}
$$
